questions.q: A dashboard loads 40 projects with one query, then runs one more query per project to count its open tasks. What is this called, and how many queries does one page view send?
questions.explain: One query for the list plus one per item is the N+1 problem. It grows with the data: 5,000 projects would mean 5,001 queries for one screen.

questions.q: The dashboard only needs, for each project, its name and how many open tasks it has. Which design sends the fewest queries and copies the least data into your process?
questions.explain: A grouped query lets the database do the counting and return only the numbers: one query, however many projects. Promise.all sends the same N+1 queries, just at the same time; loading every task copies rows you never show.
options: Load every task with tasks.findMany() and count them in JavaScript
Keep the loop, but run the counts with Promise.all
A query service method with one LEFT JOIN … GROUP BY query that returns the counts
Cache each project's count for five minutes

questions.q: When is "collect the ids, then load all related rows with one IN query" the right fix for an N+1, rather than a grouped SQL query?
questions.explain: Batch loading gives you the rows in 2 queries, which you then group in memory. When all you need is an aggregate, a GROUP BY query is cheaper still.
options: When you need the related entities themselves, for example to show each project's open tasks

questions.q: This fake database counts calls. What does the program print?
questions.explain: The loop makes 1 call for the list and 1 per project: 4. The batched version makes one call for the list and one for all the counts, however many projects there are.

questions.q: Which statement about entities and DTOs is right?
questions.explain: The entity is the full record your code works with. The response DTO is a separate shape for the network, produced by one mapper. That is why adding a private column to the entity never leaks it.
options: The entity should be sent to the client as it is, so the API always shows all the data
The repository returns entities; a mapper turns an entity into a response DTO that contains only what a client may see
A request DTO should include the id and version, so the client can choose them
DTOs are only needed when you use GraphQL

questions.q: A column costEstimate was added to the entity. What do the two mappers send?
questions.explain: The spread mapper removes the fields it knows about and publishes everything else, including any column added later. The mapper that names every field stays private by default.

questions.q: Your tasks use serial number ids. Why does interface Task extends SoftDeletableEntity { readonly id: number } fail to compile with @zudojs/database?
questions.explain: SoftDeletableEntity extends DatabaseEntity with its default string id. For number ids, extend DatabaseEntity<number> and add deletedAt: Date | null yourself.
options: Interfaces cannot extend types from packages
SoftDeletableEntity has no type parameter, so its id is a string, and number is not assignable to it
A readonly property cannot be overridden

questions.q: Which repository method is the best design for the Task API?
questions.explain: Methods named after questions keep the query boundary in one place: nobody above the repository builds filters, and certainly not from request input. Repositories return entities; mapping to JSON happens at the edge.
options: find(where: unknown), so the route can pass the query string straight in
runSql(sql: string), so services can write any query

questions.q: "Two live tasks in one project cannot have the same title." Where must this rule be enforced so that it holds even when two requests arrive at the same moment?
questions.explain: "Check, then insert" has a gap: both requests can pass the check before either inserts. Only a unique index makes the rule true. The repository then turns the violation into a 409.
options: In the route, by searching for the title before inserting
In the client, by disabling the button after one click
In the database, as a unique index; the service may still check first for a friendlier message

questions.q: Tasks are soft-deleted. Why is the index UNIQUE (project_id, lower(title)) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL better than a plain UNIQUE (project_id, title)?
questions.explain: A partial index only covers the rows that match its WHERE. Soft-deleted rows step aside, and restoring one whose title is now taken is refused with 409, which is right.
options: Deleted tasks are not covered, so a user can create a task with the title of one they deleted, and the lower() makes "Buy Milk" and "buy milk" collide
It allows two live tasks with the same title
It makes restoring a deleted task always succeed

questions.q: With @zudojs/database 1.4.0, a repository update breaks a CHECK (open_tasks >= 0) constraint and the error arrives as a 500. What is the best reading of that?
questions.explain: Constraints are the last line of defence. Validation at the edge answers 400 for bad input; a constraint firing after that means a code path the validation did not cover.
options: The client sent a bad value, so the API should answer 400 automatically
Your own code or validation let through a value the database refuses; the constraint caught a bug, so fix the code path and validate earlier
CHECK constraints should be removed because they cause 500s

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: .strict() refuses keys the schema does not know, so a client cannot choose its project through the body. .trim() removes the spaces from the valid title.

questions.q: What does normalizeLimit from @zudojs/database return for these limits?
questions.explain: A missing limit becomes the default, 20. Other values are cut to a whole number and kept between 1 and MAX_LIMIT (100). The clamp protects the database; a schema that answers 400 tells the client what it did wrong. Use both.

questions.q: What is the job of a query service such as ProjectQueries, compared with a repository?
questions.explain: Screen-shaped reads (cards, dashboards, reports) do not fit one table's repository. A query service answers them in one query and returns exactly what the screen needs.
options: It owns reads shaped for one screen: it may join and group across tables and returns DTOs, while repositories keep loading and saving entities
It is the only place allowed to open transactions

questions.q: A client may choose related data to include. Why does @zudojs/database refuse an include of project → tasks → project → tasks?
questions.explain: Includes are a way for a request to make the database do more work. Checking them against a registry of real relations, refusing cycles and capping depth keeps that work bounded.
options: It is a cycle: it could nest again and again and turn one request into an enormous response, so the relation registry rejects it (and depth is capped)
Tasks do not belong to projects
Includes are only allowed inside transactions

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: tasks → comments → author is three levels, and this call allows 2. Without the option the cap is DEFAULT_INCLUDE_DEPTH, 5.
options: RangeError - Relation include depth exceeds the maximum of 2.
RangeError - Relation include depth exceeds the maximum of 5.

questions.q: A list shows tasks newest first, 2 per page, by offset. A task is added between the two requests. What do the two pages show?
questions.explain: "Page 2" means "skip 2 rows". The new row pushed everything down one place, so C is shown twice. A deletion between the requests would make a row disappear instead.

questions.q: The same list, but page 2 means "the tasks after the last one I saw". What is printed?
questions.explain: A keyset page starts after a row, not after a count of rows. The new task E sorts before the cursor, so it does not shift the second page.

questions.q: Why does paginateCursor append the id field to your sort when it is missing?
questions.explain: A keyset cursor needs a total order. Appending the primary key as a tiebreaker makes every position unique.
options: So the response includes the id
Two rows can share a timestamp; without a unique last sort key, "the rows after this one" is not well defined and rows can be skipped or repeated
Ids are always indexed, so the query is faster

questions.q: What condition does buildKeysetWhere produce for a cursor at priority 2, id 40, sorted by priority then id, both ascending?
questions.explain: "After" in an ascending sort means a bigger priority, or the same priority and a bigger id. An AND of both "greater than" conditions would wrongly skip every row with a bigger priority but a smaller id, such as priority 3, id 7.

questions.q: What does the decoded cursor contain?
questions.explain: A keyset cursor holds only the values of the sort fields: that is all it needs to find the position, and it keeps titles and owners out of URLs. Decoding also refuses any extra field.

questions.q: An attacker hand-writes a cursor with an extra field. What happens?
questions.explain: The payload may only contain the sort fields. A bad cursor is the client's mistake, so it is a 400, and the message never repeats the cursor's contents. With a cursorSecret, an edited cursor fails the signature check first.
options: ValidationError 400 Pagination cursor contains an unexpected field.
nothing is printed; the extra field is ignored

questions.q: PostgreSQL stored a task's created_at as 10:00:00.000300. What does the cursor carry after it goes through a JavaScript Date?
questions.explain: A Date has millisecond precision, so the microseconds are lost. Rows created within the same millisecond then compare as "newer" than the cursor and are skipped. Store timestamptz(3), or sort by the id.

questions.q: Keyset pagination sorted by created_at skips rows during a bulk import. Which change fixes it?
questions.explain: The cursor's value and the stored value must be comparable exactly. Millisecond columns match a Date; an id has no precision problem at all.
options: Declare the column timestamptz(3) so the database stores only what a JavaScript Date can carry, or sort by the id instead

questions.q: The busiest query is "tasks of project X, not deleted, ordered by created_at DESC, id DESC, after a cursor, 21 rows". Which index serves it best?
questions.explain: Equality columns first, then the sort columns in the same order and direction. PostgreSQL can then jump to the project and cursor position and read 21 rows in order, with no sort step.
options: One separate index on each of the three columns

questions.q: An EXPLAIN of the task list shows Limit → Sort → Seq Scan on tasks. What does that tell you?
questions.explain: A Seq Scan reads every row, and the Sort must finish before Limit can return anything. With the right index the plan becomes Limit → Index Scan.
options: No suitable index: PostgreSQL reads the whole table and sorts it before it can return the first 21 rows
The query is wrong and returns too many rows

questions.q: Page 500 of a list, 20 per page, by LIMIT 20 OFFSET 9980, with a perfect index. About how many index entries does PostgreSQL read?
questions.explain: An offset cannot jump; it counts rows as it walks. The keyset version of the same page reads about 20, which is why deep pages and full exports should use cursors.
options: About 10,000: it must walk past every skipped row

questions.q: createTask inserts a task and then increments projects.open_tasks. What goes wrong without a transaction?
questions.explain: Related writes must be all-or-nothing. withTransaction rolls back the insert if anything after it fails, and every repository joins with withTransaction(tx).
options: Nothing, as long as both statements use parameters
If the second statement fails (or the process dies between them), the task exists but the counter was never increased, and nothing corrects it

questions.q: Inside withTransaction(client, async (tx) => { … }) a developer calls this.tasks.create(…) instead of this.tasks.withTransaction(tx).create(…). What happens?
questions.explain: @zudojs/database passes the transaction explicitly. A repository built from the root client knows nothing about tx. (The @zudojs/transactions package tracks the current transaction for you with AsyncLocalStorage.)
options: ZudoJS notices and joins the transaction automatically
The insert runs outside the transaction, so a later failure rolls back everything except that insert
Nothing changes; both forms are identical

questions.q: Two requests each complete one task and adjust a counter by reading and writing it. What is printed?
questions.explain: Both read-modify-write calls read 3 before either wrote, so both wrote 2: one decrement was lost. The atomic version reads and writes in one step, like SET open_tasks = open_tasks - 1 in SQL.

questions.q: Which repository call decreases a project's counter without a lost update, given the lesson's adapter?
questions.explain: { decrement: 1 } becomes open_tasks = open_tasks - 1, computed by PostgreSQL from the current value. Passing a number you computed from an earlier read is the read-modify-write bug.

questions.q: On a real PostgreSQL server at the default READ COMMITTED level, a developer wraps read-modify-write of the counter in withTransaction. Is the lost update fixed?
questions.explain: A transaction makes one request all-or-nothing; it does not isolate two requests from each other at READ COMMITTED. (PGlite runs one transaction at a time, which hides the bug while you test.)
options: Yes, a transaction makes other transactions wait
No: two transactions can both read the old value before either commits. Use an atomic update, a version check or a row lock

questions.q: How does optimistic concurrency with a version column stop a silent overwrite?
questions.explain: The check and the write are one statement, so there is no gap. The client that gets 409 reloads, sees the other change, and decides what to do.
options: It locks the row while the user edits
Each write includes the version it was based on in its WHERE and increments it; if someone changed the row since, nothing matches and the API answers 409
It retries the write until it succeeds
It stores every version and merges them

questions.q: When is a row lock (createLockManager(client).withRowLock(…), which uses SELECT … FOR UPDATE) a better choice than a version check?
questions.explain: A row lock makes the others wait, so it only suits work that takes milliseconds. You cannot hold a database lock while a person is typing; use a version for that.
options: For an edit form a person keeps open for ten minutes
For a short, heavily contended step inside one request, such as taking the last seat of a booking
For reads that must be fast

questions.q: A client times out and sends "complete task 5" again. The first request had already succeeded. What should completeTask do, and why?
questions.explain: Clients, proxies and users retry. Checking "already done" inside the transaction and returning early keeps the counter right however many times the request arrives.
options: Decrease the counter again, because the client asked twice
Answer 500, because this should never happen
Return the task unchanged without touching the counter: a repeated request must be harmless (idempotent)

questions.q: Which test is the most valuable for the projects and tasks data layer?
questions.explain: An invariant check catches any code path that breaks the rule, including ones you did not think of; in the lesson it found that a soft delete bypassed the counter. The same query works as a production health check.
options: That createTask calls repository.create exactly once, with a mock
After each sequence of service calls against a real database, a query confirms open_tasks equals the real number of open, not-deleted tasks
That the adapter file has no more than 150 lines

questions.q: You need an index on a table with 40 million rows that takes writes all day. Why not add CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY as a normal migration?
questions.explain: A plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes while it builds. CONCURRENTLY does not, but PostgreSQL refuses it inside a transaction block, where every @zudojs/database migration runs.
options: PostgreSQL does not support concurrent index builds
It cannot run inside a transaction, and the migration runner runs every migration in one; run it from a deploy step outside the runner
It locks the table for longer than a normal index
It only works on empty tables

questions.q: Priorities are stored as text and the list is sorted by that column. In what order do they come out?
questions.explain: Text sorts alphabetically, so "low" lands before "normal". Store a number or a PostgreSQL enum, whose order is the order you declare, and map it to words in the DTO.

questions.q: Finish toProjectCard(row). It turns a database row into the response DTO { id, name, openTasks, highPriority }, taking open and high from the row. Name every field; nothing else from the row may appear.
questions.explain: Naming each field is what keeps owner_id and internal_notes private. The as unknown as ProjectCard in the starter is exactly the kind of assertion that hides a leak from the compiler.

questions.q: Finish openCountsByProject(projectIds, openTasks). openTasks is the result of one IN query: every open task of those projects. Return a Map from each project id to its count, including projects with 0, in one pass over the tasks.
questions.explain: Start every id at 0, so projects without open tasks still appear, then count in one loop. This is the "group in memory" half of batch loading; the database part is a single projectId IN (…) query.

questions.q: Finish pageAfter(rows, cursor, limit). rows are sorted by createdAt descending, then id descending (ISO strings compare correctly as text). Return the first limit rows that come strictly after cursor ({ createdAt, id }), or from the start when cursor is null.
questions.explain: For a descending sort, "after" means an earlier date, or the same date and a smaller id. Task 3 shares a date with the cursor, and only the id tiebreaker puts it on the second page instead of losing it.

questions.q: Finish saveTitle(id, expectedVersion, title) for an in-memory store. Throw NotFoundError for a missing task and ConflictError (both from @zudojs/errors) when the version does not match. Otherwise change the title, add 1 to the version and return the task.
questions.explain: The second save was based on version 1, but the first save moved the task to version 2, so it is refused with 409 instead of silently overwriting. In SQL the check and the write are one statement: UPDATE … SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2.

questions.q: Finish findDrift(projects, tasks). Return the ids of projects whose stored openTasks differs from the number of their tasks with status "open" and deletedAt null.
questions.explain: Project 1 stores 2, but one of its open tasks was soft-deleted, so the truth is 1. This is the invariant from the lesson's tests; in SQL it is one query you can also run nightly in production.

questions.q: Write ListTasksQuery with @zudojs/schema: limit is coerced from a string to a whole number between 1 and 50, default 20; status is optional and must be "open" or "done"; unknown keys are refused. Print the parsed value, or 400 and the error message.
questions.explain: Query strings are always strings, so coerce turns "10" into 10 before the checks. An unbounded limit and an unknown sort key are both refused with 400 before any query is built.

questions.q: Finish completeTask(state, id). If the task is open, mark it done and decrease state.openTasks by 1. If it is already done, change nothing. Return the task either way.
questions.explain: Three requests for the same completion must have the effect of one. The early return for an already-done task is what makes retries and double clicks harmless.

questions.q: Write clampLimit(limit) that behaves like normalizeLimit: undefined becomes 20; any other value is cut to a whole number with Math.trunc and kept between 1 and 100.
questions.explain: A clamp guarantees the database never gets an unbounded or negative limit, whatever reaches the repository. It is a safety net under the schema, not a replacement for telling the client its limit was invalid.
